name: Gum depigmentation

lead: Gum depigmentation lightens gums that are dark because of melanin, whether from genetics or smoking. It is done as a cosmetic dental procedure.
Most published trials are small and compare one technique against another rather than against no treatment.

paras: Pigmented surface tissue is removed or ablated by scalpel, laser or chemical agents, and the gum heals with new, lighter tissue.
Wikipedia notes a longer recovery after scalpel surgery and possible side effects from chemical methods. Gums heal by secondary intention after laser treatment.

lead: Gum depigmentation is a cosmetic periodontal procedure that lightens dark (melanin-pigmented) gums, using a scalpel, laser or chemical methods.[1] Wikipedia notes that gum pigmentation is mainly linked to genetics and tobacco smoking (smoker's melanosis), with melanin made by melanocytes in the gum's basal layer.[1]
Published clinical trials, mostly small, have compared techniques such as scalpel surgery, diode and Er,Cr:YSGG lasers, microsurgery, bur-based methods and microneedling.[2][3][4][5]

paras: The Wikipedia article describes laser ablation of melanin-producing cells, scalpel removal of the pigmented layer by a periodontist or oral surgeon, and chemical methods that it says are used less today because of possible side effects.[1] Laser-treated gums heal by secondary intention.[1]

Wikipedia reports that laser treatment gives lighter, more uniform gum colour, scalpel removal takes longer to heal, and one Er,Cr:YSGG laser study showed no re-pigmentation at six months; the article is flagged for disputed neutrality and weak sourcing.[1] For smokers, it cites a study in which most patients were pigment-free about three months after quitting.[1]

Registered trials include a 40-patient comparison of surgical stripping with an Er,Cr:YSGG laser,[2] comparisons of microsurgery with diode laser or conventional scalpel techniques,[3][4] a test of ceramic trimming burs against scalpel,[5] and ongoing trials of microneedling with silymarin or platelet-rich plasma and of vitamin C or glutathione.[6][7][8] Trials of topical argan oil and coenzyme Q10 look at healing after depigmentation.[9][10] Results are not summarised here.
